analysis.one_liner: Repeals deep-water Gulf of Mexico royalty relief for oil and gas producers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2008, referred to the Senate Energy Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Energy Policy Act of 2005 gave oil and gas companies royalty relief — a break on the payments companies owe the government when they drill on federal land and waters. This bill would have repealed two of those incentives: one for natural gas from deep wells in shallow Gulf of Mexico waters, and one for deep-water production in the central and western Gulf. Killing those breaks would have meant companies paid more in royalties to the Treasury. The bill was never taken up by its own committee and died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and Gulf-state treasuries, which would collect more royalty revenue from oil and gas produced in the Gulf of Mexico, and taxpayers who ultimately fund the government with that money.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals two royalty relief incentives enacted in the Energy Policy Act of 2005: royalty incentives for natural gas from ultra-deep and deep wells in shallow Gulf waters, and royalty relief for deep-water production in the Western and Central Gulf Planning Areas [S2].
Repeals Sections 344 and 345 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005, restoring the requirement that companies pay royalties on this production [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies producing in the Gulf of Mexico, which would have resumed paying full royalties on deep-water and deep shallow-water gas production, and possibly consumers if any of the cost were passed into energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gulf of Mexico oil and gas producers

drawbacks.text: Repealing the incentives would raise production costs in the Gulf, which producers argued could reduce or delay drilling there — an objection an honest supporter would have had to weigh against the recovered revenue [S2].

The repeal is retrospective in effect for incentives companies had already relied on when bidding and planning Gulf projects, creating a fairness objection for firms that made investment decisions counting on the 2005 relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face the bill was a straightforward recovery of public money: it would have ended subsidies that let companies drill on federal waters at reduced royalty rates. The main cost-side argument is that reduced drilling in the Gulf could tighten supply, but the bill's failure means that trade-off was never publicly examined. As written, the benefits to taxpayers plausibly outweighed the costs, though the bill attracted no cosponsors and was never debated, so its design was never refined or challenged in the open.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in April 2008, and the committee — chaired by the bill's own sponsor — never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Bingaman introduced the bill by request on April 28, 2008 [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — was ever recorded [S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers in the Gulf of Mexico, who kept the deep-water royalty relief enacted in 2005 rather than resuming full royalty payments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gulf of Mexico oil and gas producers

for.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico and Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill by request and referred it to his own committee, where it received no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and it had a single sponsor with zero cosponsors, so no partisan divide was ever recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers in the Gulf of Mexico
industries.note: The bill would have repealed the 2005 royalty relief that lets these companies pay the government less than full royalties on deep-water Gulf production; killing the bill preserved that revenue break, which comes directly at the expense of the public treasury.
